title: "The paragraph, a universal unit"
jupyter: python3

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import statistics
import pandas as pd
from _outils import *          # noqa: F403
PARA = PARAGRAPHES
```

*Code covered: `tools/traduire_paragraphes.py`.*

Splitting a document before translating it is not an implementation detail: it is the
decision that determines whether the translation will be complete or cut short, and by
how much. This chapter explains the splitting that was kept — **one single assumption
about the document, and nothing else** — and the two strategies that were measured and
discarded before getting there.

An earlier version of the pipeline split notes by exploiting the exact structure of
MIMIC: a section-header pattern, a frozen translation table for the titles, detection
of laboratory blocks. It produced very good Croatian on this corpus and was
transferable nowhere. It was withdrawn in favour of the splitting described here; what
it taught is in the appendix.

## The minimal assumption

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
montre("paragraphs", ou=PARA)
```

A paragraph is a run of non-empty lines. That is all. No initial capital, no trailing
colon, no laboratory pattern, no translation table. The only thing assumed of a
document is that it contains blank lines — which is true of a MIMIC discharge summary,
of a paper, of a report, of a letter.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
montre("split", "sentences", ou=PARA)
```

`sentences()` only fires on paragraphs above the ceiling, and never cuts in the middle
of a sentence: a truncated sentence yields a **wrong** translation, not merely an
incomplete one.

What the splitting does **not** know, and that is the point:

| | old splitting, withdrawn | `traduire_paragraphes.py` |
|---|---|---|
| section-header pattern | regex specific to MIMIC | — |
| translation table for titles | 52 frozen entries | — |
| laboratory-block detector | yes | — |
| line-classification rule | 4 tests | — |
| translation direction | hard-coded EN -> HR | `--src` / `--tgt` |
| assumption about the document | full MIMIC structure | **blank lines** |

## Why the paragraph, and not something else

The answer is not aesthetic, it is measured. The paragraph is the only unit that
**survives translation**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
paragraphs = fonction("paragraphs", PARA)
src = pd.read_excel(RACINE / "CATH-LLM" / "exampleNotes_250.xlsx")[["id_note", "input"]]
hr = pd.read_csv(RACINE / "results" / "notes_croate_milmmt-12b.csv")[["id_note", "input"]]

lignes = []
for nom, d in [("English source", src), ("Croatian (MiLMMT)", hr)]:
    tailles, par_note = [], []
    for r in d.itertuples():
        p = paragraphs(r.input)
        par_note.append(len(p))
        tailles += [len(x) for x in p]
    lignes.append({"corpus": nom, "paragraphs": len(tailles),
                   "per note (median)": int(statistics.median(par_note)),
                   "median size": f"{statistics.median(tailles):.0f} chars",
                   "> 1000 chars": f"{sum(1 for t in tailles if t > 1000) / len(tailles):.1%}"})
tableau(lignes)
```

The paragraph count is **identical on both sides**. Croatian is 13 % longer in
characters — normal behaviour for the language — but it has exactly the same number of
paragraphs. Nothing in the pipeline imposed that: the blank lines are copied through as
they are, so the structure of the document crosses the translation on its own.

::: {.callout-note}
The Croatian side read here is `notes_croate_milmmt-12b.csv`, one call per paragraph.
The corpus this script produces has slightly *more* paragraphs than its input (10 471
against 10 031), because a paragraph above the character ceiling is cut into sentences
and each piece is re-joined as a paragraph of its own. The one-to-one correspondence
holds for the translation itself, not for the split/re-join round trip.
:::

A unit that is stable in both languages is what makes the splitting reversible. Neither
the line nor the sentence has that property: the line because MIMIC wraps arbitrarily
at 80 columns, the sentence because punctuation moves in translation.

## The mistake that cost a run: aiming at the context window {#sec-biais-longueur}

The natural intuition is to fill each call as much as possible: fewer calls, more
context, better translation. It is wrong, and the measurement is unambiguous.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
tableau([
    {"strategy": "whole note (1 call)", "call size": "~10,000 chars",
     "content lost": "~40 % of every note, systematically"},
    {"strategy": "filling up to 3000 chars", "call size": "3,000 chars",
     "content lost": "14 % of notes cut short, 13 % of redactions lost"},
    {"strategy": "one paragraph per call", "call size": "118 chars (median)",
     "content lost": "0 notes cut short, 2.6 % of redactions"},
])
```

### The mechanism

A translation model does not "process" a text to get the translation out. It predicts
one token at a time, and at each step it may also predict the end-of-sequence token.
**As soon as it predicts that token, generation stops and the rest of the input is
ignored.** No exception, no warning: the caller receives an answer it believes to be
complete.

Observed on a whole note: 713 tokens produced where 1,985 were allowed. The model was
not hitting a ceiling, it had stopped on its own, having translated as far as the
imaging results. The rest of the note — tijek hospitalizacije, upute pri otpustu — did
not exist in the output.

The clearest trace runs through the numbers, which a translator has to copy through
unchanged:

```
note 16292028-DS-14, split into 4 calls of 3000 characters
  call 1 (2752 chars) :  8/10 numeric values recovered
  call 2 (2987 chars) :  5/32 values recovered   <- stopped mid-piece
  call 3 (2743 chars) :  0/2  values recovered   <- nothing at all
```

### It is not the context window

The Gemma 3 architecture under MiLMMT accepts 131,072 tokens. A 10,000-character note
fits in it thirty times over. What bounds the useful input is therefore not the window,
it is the **length distribution of the training data**: these models are trained on
sentence pairs, so their comfort zone is a few hundred tokens wide.

The phenomenon is documented under the name **length bias** in document-level
translation. The wording in the literature describes the observation exactly: the
sequence stops when the end token is generated, and if the model overestimates that
token's probability, *it ignores the rest of the input and produces a truncated
translation*.

::: {.callout-important}
## Size the call on the training length, not on the window

This is the rule to take away from this chapter. The context window a model advertises
says what it can **read**, not what it can **translate in one go**. The two figures are
unrelated, and only the second matters for sizing a split.
:::

## The length ratio is blind to the worst failure

While looking for a model able to handle a whole document, Gemma 3 27B produced outputs
with ratios of 0.997 and 0.995 — apparently perfect. In reality **it was copying the
Croatian** without translating: out of 31 lines of content, 24 had stayed Croatian, 1
was English.

A copy has a ratio of 1.00. A length check therefore cannot distinguish it from a
faithful translation. A second, lexical check is needed:

```{python}
import re
CROATIAN = re.compile(r"[čćžšđ]|\b(je|su|nije|koji|nakon|prije|vam|ste|zbog|nema)\b", re.I)
ENGLISH = re.compile(r"\b(the|was|were|and|with|patient|had|for|from|discharge)\b", re.I)

for label, text in [
    ("untranslated copy", "Bolesnik je primljen nakon prometne nesreće, bez komplikacija."),
    ("real translation ", "The patient was admitted after a traffic accident, with no complications."),
]:
    print(f"  {label} : croatian={bool(CROATIAN.search(text))} "
          f"english={bool(ENGLISH.search(text))}")
```

Two lessons: a metric of quantity does not replace a metric of nature, and an indicator
that cannot fail measures nothing.

## Sizing for the target machine

The intended production machine is an **A100 40 GB**. MiLMMT in bf16 weighs 24 GB, so
16 GB are left for the KV cache and the activations — which is what bounds the batch
size.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
montre("plan_vram", ou=PARA)
```

The function runs **before** the model is loaded, and it rejected a first setting
straight away:

```
expected VRAM: weights 24 GB + KV cache 11.6 GB (32 x 920 tokens) = ~41 GB / 40 GB target
  WARNING: exceeds the target. Reduce --batch to ~31 or pass --four-bit
```

### The KV cache, term by term {#sec-cache-kv}

The item people forget is the KV cache, and it is worth writing out in full, because
the shape of the formula is the whole argument:

```
KV cache = 2 (K and V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × length × batch × 2 bytes
         = 2 × 48 × 8 × 256 × 920 × 24 × 2
         = 8.7 GB
```

Every factor but the last two is fixed by the architecture: MiLMMT-46-12B has 48
layers, 8 key-value heads and a head dimension of 256. That leaves **0.39 MB of cache
per token**, and two levers, both strictly linear: **the sequence length** and **the
batch size**. Double either one and the cache doubles.

Two consequences follow, and they are the reason this section exists:

- the cache stays in **bf16 even when the weights are quantised**. Quantisation applies
  to the weights, not to the cached activations — a 4-bit model drops from 24 GB to
  7 GB of weights while keeping a full-size cache. At batch 64 the cache reaches
  23.2 GB, more than three times the weights;
- **`--max-chars` is not the knob to turn when VRAM is tight.** The 1000-character
  ceiling exists to protect the translation (see @sec-biais-longueur), not the memory,
  and 95 % of calls never come near it — the median call is 118 characters. The knob
  that actually moves the cache is `--batch`, which is precisely what `plan_vram`
  suggests reducing.

Two settings that are valid on 40 GB:

| | weights | batch | KV cache | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bf16 | 24 GB | 24 | 8.7 GB | ~38 GB |
| 4-bit | 7 GB | 64 | 23.2 GB | ~35 GB, slower per token |

::: {.callout-warning}
The 15 % activation margin is an estimate, not a measurement. On the real run one GPU
climbed to 41.4 GB where the function announced 38 — the gap is entirely down to that
flat margin. On an A100 40 GB the batch therefore has to come down, or the run has to
go 4-bit. The estimate stays useful for eliminating absurd settings; it does not
replace the measured peak.
:::

## More faithful, and faster

Splitting by paragraph is **both more faithful and faster** than filling up to 3,000
characters. Faster may be surprising: a batch of 24 short paragraphs saturates the GPU
better than a batch of 4 long pieces, because a batch generates until its longest
sequence finishes. Optimising the call size upwards therefore lost on both counts at
once.

## Takeaways

- One single assumption — the document contains blank lines — is enough to split any
  corpus. All the rest of the MIMIC machinery is optional.
- The paragraph is the right unit because it is **stable under translation**: 10,031
  paragraphs in English, 10,031 in the Croatian of `notes_croate_milmmt-12b.csv`.
- Sizing a call on the context window is a category error. What counts is the length
  seen during training.
- A model that stops too early raises no error: it ignores the rest of the input. Only
  an explicit check catches it.
- The length ratio does not distinguish a translation from a copy. You have to measure
  the **language** of the output, not only its size.
- The KV cache is linear in sequence length and in batch size, and stays in bf16 even
  with 4-bit weights. `--batch` is the lever; `--max-chars` protects the translation,
  not the memory.
- Filling calls to the maximum lost on fidelity *and* on speed.
